Friday, 11:50 pm

Day two of the New Me plan, and it's already dead.

After the maths paper on Wednesday I came home furious with myself. I wrote a timetable in red pen: sleep at 9 pm, wake at 4 am, study two hours before school. Starting the very next day. Dolma said, "Mehak, you sleep at one. That's a huge jump." I told her she didn't get it.

Thursday I lay in bed at nine staring at the fan till past midnight. Alarm at four. Hit snooze till six. Slept through chemistry.

Tonight I didn't even try. I'm writing this at midnight and I feel like the biggest failure. Two days. I couldn't even do two days.

Maybe Dolma was right. Maybe the plan was the failure, not me. I don't know. I'm too tired to know.

Dear Seema,

You asked how I finally stopped lying awake till two. Promise not to laugh: it was a rule I wrote on a sticky note.

"IF it's 10 pm, THEN the phone goes to the charger in the kitchen." That's it. No arguing with myself. Before, I'd say "just five more minutes" and suddenly it was midnight.

Then a short routine that's always the same: wash my face, brush teeth, lay out tomorrow's uniform, and read a paper book for twenty minutes. Same order every night.

The first week I kept reaching for the phone that wasn't there. It felt silly. By the second week, washing my face started to make me yawn, like my brain knew what came next.

I'm sleeping by 10:45 most nights now. Try it. Pick your own "if" and write it down.

Pema

You want the secret, Yamini? It's not a secret. It's a sentence.

I'm Kiran. Last year I was sleeping at one, two, sometimes later. I'd tell myself I'd stop scrolling "soon", and soon never came. My mum finally said, "You need a rule, not a wish."

So I made one: if the clock says ten, then the phone goes on the shelf in the hallway. Not in my room. Not under my pillow. The hallway.

Then after that, the same small things every night. Hot water on my face. Change into old pyjamas. Read one chapter of whatever novel. Lights off.

For the first few nights my brain was annoyed. It kept thinking of messages I might be missing. But after about ten days, just splashing my face made me yawn. My body had learned the order.

Now I'm usually asleep by eleven. That's all it took: one if and one then.

My name's Hrithik, and I share a room with my cousin Karthik in our hostel. This term I noticed something new on his desk every evening: a tall can of energy drink, sometimes two, next to a steel glass of strong tea.

"Keeps me sharp," he said, when I asked. He'd drink them around seven or eight, then study till late.

But he wasn't sharp. He'd lie in bed till two, tossing, the light from his phone on the ceiling. At six, when the bell went, he'd groan and pull the pillow over his head.

In the mornings he looked grey. By lunch he was buying another can. Once in class he put his head down and our teacher had to call his name twice.

I don't know exactly what was going on inside him. But the cans kept multiplying, and he seemed more tired every week.

I'm Vasudha, and I share a desk with Tanuja in Class 11. At the start of the month she started carrying a small blue notebook with columns drawn in pencil. Every morning, before assembly, she'd write in it: two times and a number.

I finally asked. She showed me: "Bed", "Up", and "Focus 1 to 5". Some days she'd slept at 1 and woken at 6:30. Focus: 2. Other days, bed at 11, up at 6:30. Focus: 4 or 5.

After two weeks she spread the pages on the desk and circled the 4s and 5s. Almost all were nights with seven or eight hours.

"I kept telling myself I work better tired," she said, tapping the page. "The notebook says I don't."

The next week I noticed she left our study group at 10:15. I can't say for sure what changed in her head. But her notebook had more 4s.

Day 15: She sat on the balcony with the notebook and a highlighter. Every 4 and 5 sat next to a night of seven or eight hours. Every 1 and 2 followed a short night.

"Okay," she said aloud. "It's not willpower. It's sleep."

Chetan leaned over the page. "Huh. That's actually clear." That night she was in bed by eleven, without anyone telling her.

In Kherwadi village, the school bus left at 7:15, and for months Trisha had missed it twice a week. She'd lie awake till past midnight, then sleep through her mother's calls.

Her older cousin Sunaina, home from nursing college, gave different advice from everyone else. "Don't fight the night. Fix the morning."

So Trisha set a wake time of 6 am, every day, even on the Sunday of the village fair. The first thing she did was step out into the courtyard and throw open the shutters so the early light came in. Then she walked to the well and back with the buffalo, ten minutes. Then a proper breakfast of poha with her grandfather.

The first week, she yawned all day. By the third week, she was tired by ten at night without trying. She hadn't missed the bus in twelve days.

But then I thought, one bad week isn't the whole month. It's just a week. So the very next morning I set the alarm for 6:30 again. I was a zombie that day. But I got up.

Within four days I was back. Slipping isn't failing. Stopping is.

Mohit, sit with your Chandrika bua for a minute. I know your marks came today. Let me tell you about mine, when I was sixteen.

My Class 10 results came, and science was far lower than I'd hoped. That same evening I told my father, "I'm leaving school. I'll join the tailoring shop." I meant it. I felt like the whole town knew.

My father didn't argue. He only said, "Decide in three days. Not tonight."

So that night I cried. The next day I walked to my friend Kamala's house and we sat on her steps eating guavas, saying nothing much. I didn't open a single book or make a single plan.

On the third day, the shock had faded. I could see it was one subject, not my whole life. I stayed in school.

So tonight, beta, just feel it. Decide nothing big till the weekend.

Her hands shook. "I'm dropping commerce," she texted her friend Alka. "I'll do something else. Anything."

Alka called immediately. "Don't decide today. Seriously. Come over."

It was snowing, and the buses weren't running, so Dilnaz walked twenty minutes through slush. At Alka's house they sat by the bukhari with kahwa. Dilnaz cried, then talked, then was quiet.

"Today you feel it," Alka said. "Tomorrow you think."

That night Dilnaz wrote only one line in her diary: No decisions till Friday.

On Friday, calmer, she saw the re-exam date on the notice board and started planning for it instead.

In the small town of Nagaur, Jaya had scored 41 out of 80 in the Class 10 mathematics pre-board, and she'd expected at least 60. Instead of crying about it for a week, she asked her teacher, Jatin Sir, for the answer sheet back.

That evening she spread it on the charpai in the courtyard with three coloured pens. Red for questions she didn't know how to do. Blue for silly mistakes: a wrong sign, a copied number. Green for questions left blank or rushed.

Red: 7 marks. Blue: 9 marks. Green: 23 marks.

She stared. Almost all the green was the last section. She'd spent forty minutes on the first two questions and then raced through the rest.

Next morning she showed Jatin Sir. He nodded. "So it's mostly time, not knowledge." They agreed she'd practise full papers with a watch every Sunday.

qa.q: How many marks were lost to questions left blank or rushed?
qa.a: Green: 23 marks.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt when she saw the green total?
qa.a: She probably felt surprised and a bit relieved, realising most of the loss came from timing, not from not knowing the maths.

qa.q: What else could Jaya do alongside the Sunday timed papers?
qa.a: She could set a time limit per section on the paper itself, so she moves on instead of spending forty minutes on two questions.

qa.q: How does Jaya's analysis look to Jatin Sir?
qa.a: Jatin Sir likely feels encouraged, since she came with a clear breakdown instead of excuses, which makes it easy to plan practice together.

grounding: Shows a student reviewing her answer sheet, sorting lost marks into knowledge gaps, careless errors and time trouble, and finding time management caused most of the loss.

In Prague, Jana got her maths exam back with a grade she had never seen before: a four. Her friend Dalia found her on the tram stop bench, staring at it.

"I studied," Jana said. "I actually studied."

"Then let's see where it went," Dalia said.

At the café near school, they spread the paper out. Jana made three columns on a napkin: didn't know it, careless, ran out of time. They went question by question.

Didn't know it: two small questions, 6 points. Careless: a minus sign, a misread graph, 5 points. Ran out of time: the whole last section, 18 points.

Jana sat back. "I spent half the exam on question three because I wanted it perfect."

Dalia tapped the napkin. "So it's not that you're bad at maths. It's the clock."

Jana folded the napkin into her pencil case, looking lighter.

qa.q: How many points did Jana lose by running out of time?
qa.a: 18 points, the whole last section.

qa.q: How did Jana feel before and after the analysis?
qa.a: Before, she felt stunned and discouraged, having studied hard; afterwards she looked lighter, relieved that the main problem was the clock.

qa.q: What could Jana practise next, based on the columns?
qa.a: She could do timed practice papers and set a limit for each question, so she stops chasing perfection on one question and reaches the last section.

qa.q: How might Dalia see her part in that afternoon?
qa.a: Dalia probably feels glad and useful, having turned her friend's shock into a clear breakdown over a café table.

grounding: Shows a student sorting lost marks into knowledge gaps, careless errors and time trouble, and finding poor time management in the last section caused most of the loss.
